commentary.bottom_line: Fourteen prospective pilots with real users reported tool performance, safety events, and usability during limited deployment, and several surfaced problems such as falling adoption or unanalyzable exams. No study compared piloting with direct full rollout, so whether piloting prevents population-wide harm has not been tested.

perspectives.view: Two RCTs and nine prospective comparator studies evaluated AI tools inside limited real deployments, and most reported favorable results. These designs compare the tool with usual care rather than comparing a pilot strategy with immediate full rollout. Certainty for the practice is low because of this indirectness, single-site designs, and the possibility that successful pilots are published more often.

Several pilots measured error rates before full rollout. The surgical triage tool had specificity of 0.74, and LLM misclassification accounted for 2 of 19 false-negative cases. iAorta identified 21 of 22 aortic syndrome cases. In one 100-patient pilot, real-time supervisors did not need to stop any consultation, which suggests supervision during a pilot may help contain harm.

Pilots reported workflow findings that earlier testing did not show. In an Israeli emergency department, adoption fell from 68% to 30% and length of stay was 4.9 h in both wings. A staged deployment with over 13,000 consented users identified challenges not apparent in initial testing. In a handheld echo pilot, 71.8% of attempts were analyzable.

One pilot enrolled 50 non-English-speaking patients in China, and another enrolled 120 older adults. A Thai community hospital pilot of 1,375 patients reported no system failure. No pilot reported Medicaid, U.S. safety-net, or low-literacy participants, so pilots conducted elsewhere may miss failures specific to those groups.

FDA draft lifecycle guidance describes a one-month deployment on a patient subset before site-wide use, and CHAI playbooks treat piloting as a requirement for high-risk tools. Both are recommendations rather than binding rules. Only one pilot in this set took place in the United States.

The supplied summaries report no pilot cost, staffing, or time needed to reach a rollout decision. Pilot sizes ranged from 50 to 13,846 patients, which suggests there is no shared standard for scope. The adoption decline in the Israeli pilot suggests pilots may need to run long enough to observe sustained use.

In a 100-patient pilot, safety supervisors watched every AI interaction in real time and patients reported high satisfaction. This design kept a human available during each consultation. The staged deployment enrolled over 13,000 consented users, which indicates participants in that pilot agreed to take part.

commentary.research_gap: No study compared sites or units that piloted a tool with those that deployed at full scale, so the effect of piloting on harm, rework, or tool abandonment is unknown. Future studies should also report pilot duration, sample size, stop criteria, the problems found, and the changes made before rollout.
commentary.underserved_note: One pilot included 50 non-English-speaking patients in China, and one Thai community hospital pilot reported no system failure. No pilot reported Medicaid, U.S. safety-net, or low-literacy participants. Health systems serving those groups have no direct evidence that pilots at other sites will surface the problems their patients may face, which suggests the pilot itself should include them.
